Samsung Electronics to Mass-Produce 'Dream Semiconductor' Silicon Photonics by 2028

Samsung Electronics' foundry division has unveiled a roadmap to begin mass production of silicon photonics — dubbed the "dream semiconductor" — starting in 2028. The company plans to accelerate its pursuit of industry leader TSMC through a "turnkey" strategy that bundles silicon photonics with high-bandwidth memory (HBM), system semiconductor foundry services, and advanced packaging.

According to industry sources on the 29th, Samsung Electronics presented this strategy at the OFC 2026 conference held in Los Angeles on March 17th. Silicon photonics is a technology that transmits and receives data using light rather than electricity. Compared to current methods that rely on copper interconnects, it offers dramatically higher speeds and is drawing attention as a solution to the data bottleneck problem — one of the key pain points in AI semiconductors.

Samsung will focus through next year on securing foundational silicon photonics technology and platforms — specifically integrating a photonic integrated circuit (PIC), which converts light into electricity, with an electronic integrated circuit (EIC) that precisely controls that electrical signal, combining them to function as a single chip.

Full integration with AI semiconductors is set to begin in 2028, with silicon photonics chips mounted alongside the "switch chip" — the first point of entry for external data. This architecture is similar to NVIDIA's Spectrum-X product line, developed in partnership with TSMC last year. By 2029, the scope expands further, with silicon photonics incorporated into packaging that combines a GPU — responsible for AI computation — with HBM.

The driving motivation behind Samsung's push into this technology is securing global Big Tech companies as foundry customers. While commercialization of silicon photonics is still in its early stages, major semiconductor firms have identified it as a next-generation core technology. NVIDIA in particular has been the most aggressive mover in this space — CEO Jensen Huang has referenced silicon photonics at every major public appearance since last year, and recently committed $2 billion to Lumentum, a silicon photonics-focused company, to secure related technology.

It is widely observed that Samsung's foundry division must rapidly build out silicon photonics mass-production capabilities in order to be well-positioned to win next-generation orders from semiconductor customers.

Based on the roadmap Samsung has disclosed, the company remains approximately three years behind TSMC in terms of technology maturity. Samsung's strategy is to differentiate itself from TSMC through the turnkey approach — building an integrated mass-production system encompassing memory (HBM), system semiconductors, advanced packaging, and now silicon photonics, none of which TSMC offers under a single roof. The pitch to customers centers on shorter production lead times and lower costs.

As one industry official put it: "The real head-to-head battle with TSMC begins the moment Samsung starts applying silicon photonics in actual mass production."

▶ Global AI Optical Transceiver Market to Reach US$26 Billion in 2026; Component Shortages Identified as Primary Capacity Expansion Bottleneck — TrendForce

• TrendForce expects the global AI optical transceiver market to expand from US$16.5 billion in 2025 to US$26 billion in 2026, representing 57% YoY growth.

• This acceleration reflects not only specification upgrades but also a structural reshaping of the optical communications supply chain, driven by the faster pace of AI data center buildouts.

• As AI data center expansion continues, demand for 800G-and-above optical transceivers — used for interconnects between AI server clusters — is surging.

• North American CSP data center traffic is sustaining annual growth of over 30%, with aggressive GPU and AI server deployments by major cloud players driving high growth in high-speed optical interconnects.

• However, constrained production capacity for core optoelectronic chips such as EMLs and CW-LDs is deepening supply shortages, acting as the primary bottleneck for overall optical transceiver capacity expansion.

• In addition, high-precision manufacturing processes such as optical alignment are difficult to scale, and the pace of productivity improvement faces structural limits.

• At the same time, the rising power consumption and heat dissipation challenges of high-speed optical modules are increasing system design complexity, adding pressure on actual data center deployment and mass-production schedules.

• Upstream suppliers, led by NVIDIA and key system vendors, are shifting their procurement strategies — adopting strategic long-term agreements (LTAs) to secure critical components and reduce dependence on short-term spot-market purchases, thereby mitigating supply risk.

• TrendForce emphasizes that growth in the AI optical transceiver market is shifting from a single-product upgrade narrative toward three axes: market expansion, generational technology transitions, and application diversification.

• As 1.6T-generation products gradually enter mass production, demand for edge computing and data center interconnect (DCI) applications is expected to rise, fueling growth in the 800G and 1.6T ZR/ZR+ coherent optical module market.

• In response to component shortages, major international players such as Coherent, Lumentum, and AAOI — along with Taiwanese firms including ELASER and LuxNet Corporation — are moving to expand capacity and adopt new technologies.

• 2026–2027 will be a critical window for establishing positions in the 1.6T supply chain, with success in design-ins at tier-1 customers expected to be the decisive factor for future market share.

GF Overseas Electronics & Communications

☄ Lumentum (LITE US, Buy): Earnings Preview — Outlook Becoming More Certain

☀ Maintain Buy rating; raise target price to US$1,174:
We forecast FY3Q/FY4Q26 revenue of US$840 million / US$1.02 billion, versus consensus of US$830 million / US$970 million. We estimate EPS of US$2.4 / US$3.1, versus consensus of around US$2.3 / US$2.7. We expect earnings visibility to improve further as laser capacity approaches being largely booked out through 2028, alongside tightening EML supply and stronger pricing power. Accordingly, we raise our CY26/CY27 EPS estimates to US$13 / US$31. To reflect improved medium- to long-term visibility, we roll our valuation forward to CY28 and raise our target price to US$1,174, based on 20x CY28 P/E.

☀ Structural supply tightness, combined with improving demand visibility, strengthens EML pricing:
Upstream laser supply remains structurally tight. The increase in prepayments from optical module makers in 1Q indicates that lasers continue to be in short supply. We expect laser capacity to be largely booked out through 2028. Given the limited number of suppliers and the long lead times required for capacity expansion, we believe EML prices still have room to rise.

☀ CPO / NPO / OCS:
Although the market has recently been discussing CPO yield issues, we believe the industry trend remains intact. At the same time, visibility is improving for NPO solutions in CSP ASICs. As NPO/CPO solutions begin to scale, laser suppliers should fully benefit from their critical position in the value chain. In addition, Google recently disclosed at its conference the use of OCS in TPU v8i, enabling a cluster-level, high-radix, reconfigurable optical interconnect architecture to improve network utilization and system scalability. We expect OCS to be adopted by more cloud service providers over time.
